summary:
Ayacucho stands under Peru's national framework. No department-specific trans statute, ordinance, enforcement action or incident series for Ayacucho appears in the sources, and all attached material is national in scope, so the operative facts for a visitor to the region are the national ones.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity or consensual same-sex sexual activity, lawful since the 1924 Penal Code, and the age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation under a 2012 Constitutional Court decision. Legal protection against discrimination and hate crime on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is absent: Government Decree Nº 1323 had criminalised such discrimination from 7 January 2017 through Articles 46 and 323 of the Penal Code, Congress voted 66–29 in May 2017 to strip those provisions, and the protections were subsequently removed as the Penal Code was reworked. Peru is one of only three countries in South America, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage.

Access to public facilities matching gender identity is restricted by law. The congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved on 20 February 2025 a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, and the Plenary approved it and exempted it from a second vote on 2 April 2025. Its article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their biological sex, with exceptions only for custody, where medical attention is required, or for accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities; it also bans ambiguous bathroom signage. The stated trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport.

Law 32331, enacted 13 May 2025, bars trans people from using public restrooms according to their gender identity and bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. The IDEHPUCP human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru finds the restriction openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their identity, implicitly casting trans people as harassment risks, and it invokes Inter-American Court of Human Rights Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, under which gender identity falls within protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The institute also records dehumanising comparisons made by congressman Lizarzaburu on the floor.

Legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of IDEHPUCP of 15 April 2025 argues that article 5 violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, and that the stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype implicitly presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho warns that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including identity checks, and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms.

The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents extends the restriction. Human Rights Watch reports that it mandates public-restroom entry be determined by biological sex, barring trans people including trans youth from facilities matching their identity; that its vaguely worded child-protection articles, notably Article 4 on media and advertising and Article 5, enable censorship of identity-related, artistic and educational content; and that the minimum sentence for obscenity rose from three to four years. Human Rights Watch characterises child protection as a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Violence against trans people is rising and recorded figures understate it. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report, covered on 22 July 2024, records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases over 2020–2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023, 12 of them trans women, from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty, and the violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 denuncias in 2020. The report recounts the February 2023 gang abduction of trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and her killing in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme. A July 2024 report finds hate crimes increasing with trans women most affected, and co-author Gianna Camacho states that recorded numbers are only a sub-registry.

The torture and rape of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, ended in conviction on 15 December 2025: police officers Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León received 17 years' imprisonment, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It is Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.
tangentialFactors:
Peru is one of only three South American countries, alongside Paraguay and Guyana, without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage, and Outright International reports that public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, struck an anti-equality decree as unconstitutional. An April 2025 law on foreign funding of NGOs lets authorities revoke registrations on public order and security grounds, which risks being weaponised against queer organising.

In April 2025 the television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed the first openly-lesbian congresswoman, Susel Paredes, telling her to go use the men's room. The IDEHPUCP also records dehumanising comparisons made on the congressional floor during the restroom debate, indicating official hostility in the legislative setting.

A 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study found that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work, a documented exposure factor for police and public violence. Extrapolating from capital-city data to Ayacucho is not supported by the sources; the figure is context for national patterns of exposure rather than a regional estimate.
localsOnly:
Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity. In 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published 8 November, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced on 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

Healthcare classifications have shifted in both directions. In May 2024 the government decreed transsexualism a mental health problem in order to cover trans healthcare; after protests, MINSA revised the term to gender discordance in June 2024 for health-insurance classification purposes, and in June 2024 health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described by Human Rights Watch as a step toward dignity for trans patients.

Conversion therapy is banned in Peru for medical professionals, and in May 2024 MINSA reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases, a protection with direct bearing on trans and LGBTQ minors exposed to such practices. Residents nevertheless live without statutory anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection, since the Penal Code provisions introduced by Decree Nº 1323 were removed.
